newsitem.title: JAPAN: Issues in Japan's October 20 general elections.
newsitem.headline: Issues in Japan's October 20 general elections.

text.p: The following are some of the key issues in Japan's general election held on Sunday, with the views of the major parties:
SALES TAX: The bungled introduction of a three percent sales tax on all goods and services cost prime minister Noboru Takeshita his job in 1989.
Since then the tax has become more or less accepted by the public but the controversy is back with a scheduled increase in the levy to five percent next year.

Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) - Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's LDP says it would abide by a government decision to raise the tax to five percent next April and implement cuts in government spending and administrative reform.

Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) - The main opposition party, led by Ichiro Ozawa, vehemently opposes the rise, saying it would keep the tax at three percent and also introduce large-scale income tax cuts of 18 trillion yen ($161 billion).
Democrats - The new Democratic Party led by the liberal and dovish Yukio Hatoyama accepts the scheduled rise, but says it would compensate pensioners and the poor through subsidies.
The Socialists and the small Sakigake party have called for a review, including a lower sales tax for food. The Communists say they would scrap the tax altogether.

BUREAUCRACY: All parties have made streamlining government a plank in their campaign platforms following a series of bank failures and mortgage firm scandals involving the powerful Finance Ministry and complaints that the Health Ministry allowed hundreds of haemophiliacs to be infected with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, through contaminated blood products.
The LDP says it would halve the 22 ministries and government agencies.
Shinshinto calls for an across-the-board 25 percent reduction in civil servants and a drastic cut in the overall number of local governments.

The Democrats, whose co-leader Naoto Kan as health minister spearheaded the probe into the AIDS scandal, has pledged to reduce government to eight ministries and inaugurate a bureaucracy watchdog in parliament.

The Socialists favour decentralisation, freedom of information and measures to cut government debt. The Communists call for free medication and welfare paired with cuts in public and military spending. Sakigake says it would take part in a new government pursuing administrative reform.

OKINAWA AND U.S.-JAPAN SECURITY - An outcry against the concentration of U.S. bases on Okinawa was triggered by the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl last year by three U.S. servicemen. In a provincial referendum last month, an overwhelming majority voted for further reduction of the bases.
The LDP aims to strengthen security ties with the United States. The party promises further reductions in U.S. bases on Okinawa and support for the island's sagging economy.
Shinshinto has also called for strengthening security ties with the United States and a law spelling out the exact terms of the alliance. It also favours streamlining bases on Okinawa.
The Democrats were the first non-leftist party to announce they would eventually seek a U.S. troop withdrawal in some 20 years, although keeping intact the security alliance.
The Socialists would cut military spending and reduce bases on Okinawa, an approach shared by Sakigake. The Communists would abolish military ties with the United States altogether. ($1=112 yen)
